summary: Your report is a strong, tightly argued case: explicit stakeholder and option analysis, a defensible decision rule, four well-used case studies and targeted recommendations. All criteria are at Excellent. To sustain that level, tighten a few details: the WannaCry figure, the characterisation of the known defect risk, the decision-rule wording, and direct analysis of health-contract failure modes.
next_steps: Correct the WannaCry extent in 'Arguments against shipping' to 80 of 236 trusts affected (NAO) and check the 19,000 appointments figure against the same source.

In 'How should Rachel decide when to ship?', distinguish partial test data from full test coverage and reword decision-rule step 2 so 'tolerable' aligns with AS ISO 31000 risk-acceptance practice rather than 'no harm to people'.
In DISCUSSION, add direct analysis of hospital/emergency-service failure modes for the health contract instead of relying mainly on ransomware and radiotherapy analogies.

criteria.C1: You identify three distinct ethical issues—risk-driven testing, treating data loss as harmless, and conflict of interest/undisclosed defects—and link them to engineering design and organisational context (six-month cadence, revenue, decision authority). Your stakeholder table gives interests and the decision each controls, including patients who cannot consent. This meets the Excellent descriptor; to keep it there, ensure each stakeholder's interest is tied explicitly to one of the named issues.
criteria.C2: Your for-and-against arguments are genuine and rebutted with reasons, not opinion—the competitor argument in 'Arguments for shipping' is answered by the health department's ability to choose when told failure rates. Conclusions target Rachel, management, the health department, the chip supplier and design engineers. This is Excellent; to sustain it, align decision-rule step 2 in 'How should Rachel decide when to ship?' with AS ISO 31000 risk acceptance.
criteria.C3: Your structure is logical—issues, stakeholder map, arguments for, arguments against, decision rule, option comparison, conclusion—and Table 2 allocates risk to each stakeholder so the conclusion follows from the argument. The option table and Figure 1 support the flow. This is Excellent; to keep it there, add direct health-contract failure-mode analysis in DISCUSSION so the conclusion rests on the scenario as well as the analogies.
criteria.C4: You use eight credible references and four external cases (WannaCry, Therac-25, Pentium, Volkswagen), balancing qualitative reasoning with quantitative evidence such as the US$475 million Pentium charge. You also acknowledge where analogies do not transfer. This is Excellent; to sustain it, correct the WannaCry extent to 80 of 236 trusts (NAO) and verify the 19,000 appointments figure against the same source.
criteria.C5: All required sections serve their functions, with an abstract of roughly the required length, two informative tables and Figure 1 used substantively. Prose is fluent, concise and largely error-free; IEEE references are consistently structured and relevant. This is Excellent; to keep it there, ensure the WannaCry statistic and decision-rule wording are corrected so the text and tables remain fully consistent.
